blocks.content: docker history shows you every layer an image is built from, in order, along with the exact command that created each one and how much size it added. It is one of the fastest ways to understand why an image is the size it is.
Running docker history against any image prints a table: one row per layer, the (often truncated) Dockerfile instruction that produced it, and the size that layer added to the image.

blocks.alt: One row per layer, in build order

blocks.content:
docker history myapp:1.0
# IMAGE       CREATED BY                        SIZE
# 9f2a1b3c    CMD ["node" "index.js"]          0B
# 3d4e5f6a    COPY . .                          42MB
# 1a2b3c4d    RUN npm install                   210MB
# ...         FROM node:18                      994MB

blocks.content: 2. Finding Where the Size Actually Comes From
blocks.text: 2. Finding Where the Size Actually Comes From

blocks.content: When an image is unexpectedly large, docker history is the first tool to reach for. It is common to discover a single RUN instruction (an unnecessary package install, a build tool never cleaned up afterward) responsible for the majority of the image's weight.

blocks.alt: A single oversized layer is usually the real culprit

blocks.content: 3. History Reflects the Build, Not Runtime
blocks.text: 3. History Reflects the Build, Not Runtime

blocks.content: It is worth being precise about what history shows: the layers baked in at build time, from the Dockerfile. Any changes a running container makes to its writable layer at runtime do not show up here at all, docker history is strictly about how the image itself was assembled.

blocks.alt: This is build-time history, not a log of runtime activity

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker history lists every layer with the instruction and size behind it, in the order they were built.
It is the fastest way to diagnose an unexpectedly large image, one oversized layer is usually the actual cause.
